We should first spend a focused six to eight weeks improving utilisation of what we already own, and only revisit procurement if that effort demonstrably fails.

The case starts with cost, and it's worth being honest about the numbers. A meaningful capacity addition — two or three high-end accelerators plus the supporting power, cooling, and rack space — would run well into six figures once you include the operational overhead. That money is not free. It competes directly with hiring, with data licensing, and with the customer-facing work that actually generates revenue. Meanwhile, our utilisation telemetry tells a less flattering story than the queue times suggest: averaged across the week, our GPUs sit idle roughly 60 percent of the time. The pain is real, but it is a scheduling and allocation problem as much as a capacity problem. We are experiencing congestion, not scarcity, and those have very different remedies.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and I want to acknowledge it properly. Interactive work — notebook experimentation, model debugging, quick inference tests — suffers disproportionately when hardware is contended. An engineer who waits forty minutes for a GPU loses flow, and flow is where a lot of our creative engineering happens. But the fix for interactive latency is not necessarily more silicon; it's better partitioning. Reserving a slice of the fleet for interactive use, with batch and training jobs filling the remainder, would protect the developer experience at a fraction of the cost of new hardware. If we find that the reserved slice is saturated even while the batch pool idles, that is exactly the evidence we'd need to justify expansion — and we'd know precisely how much to buy.

Reliability cuts in favour of restraint, too. Adding hardware doesn't just add capacity; it adds failure surface. Every new card, cable, and power feed is something that can degrade silently or fail loudly, and our current monitoring is calibrated to the fleet we have. There's also a subtler reliability benefit to running leaner: a fleet operated at high utilisation with good scheduling discipline is a fleet whose true capacity limits we understand. Teams that paper over scheduling problems with purchases tend to discover, at the worst possible moment, that they don't actually know how their infrastructure behaves under load.

The opportunity cost and reversibility arguments point the same direction. Capital spent on GPUs is capital not spent elsewhere, and hardware depreciates quickly in a market where model efficiency improvements routinely halve the compute needed for a given task. Buying now locks in today's assumptions about our workload mix. If we buy hardware and it turns out we didn't need it, that money is gone.

Utilisation numbers can mislead — a GPU that's "idle" may be idle because a critical job just finished and the next one is queued behind a human, not because capacity is free. If we miss them, we'll have the data to size the purchase correctly rather than guessing.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward on its face. Our inference queues spike hard during business hours, and during those windows we occasionally see requests waiting longer than our latency SLO allows. Adding capacity is the obvious lever: it's fast to reason about, it makes the pain go away immediately, and our finance contact has signalled that capital is available this quarter. But that simplicity is deceptive. New accelerators carry a real total cost beyond the invoice — rack power, cooling, networking, and the engineering time to integrate and operate them. More importantly, our own telemetry tells us our fleet sits at roughly 35–40% average utilisation across the week. We are, in effect, proposing to solve a scheduling problem by buying our way out of it, and paying a premium to do so. Every dollar spent on idle silicon is a dollar not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. That opportunity cost is the quiet killer here: it never shows up on a capacity dashboard, but it compounds.

The case for improving utilisation is less glamorous but stronger. Most of our low utilisation stems from three things: batch sizes tuned conservatively months ago, models pinned to specific nodes for convenience rather than efficiency, and a scheduling policy that treats every workload as if it were latency-critical when in fact only a subset are. If we introduce workload tiering — interactive requests getting priority and dedicated headroom, batch jobs filling the gaps — we can likely push utilisation into the 60–70% range without users noticing anything except that nothing changed. Latency for interactive traffic should actually *improve*, because the noisy batch jobs that currently compete with them would be shunted to off-peak windows. Reliability improves too: a fleet running at 40% has far more headroom to absorb node failures, and we can take machines down for maintenance without degrading service. A fleet running hot at 85% because we bought more and then grew into it has none of that slack.

There's also the question of reversibility, which I think we've underweighted. Hardware purchases are close to irreversible at our scale. The market for used accelerators is thin, depreciation is steep, and if our inference demand shifts — say, a model change cuts our compute needs per request by half, or a vendor API becomes good enough that we offload a class of workloads — we'll be carrying stranded capacity for years. Utilisation work, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible. Tuning schedulers, re-tiering workloads, and adjusting batch sizes cost engineering time and nothing else, and every lesson learned transfers to whatever hardware we eventually buy. If we do purchase later, we'll do it with a much sharper sense of what we actually need.

My utilisation estimates come from coarse instrumentation, and it's possible that a deeper look reveals our peak-hour profile is genuinely capacity-bound, in which case no amount of scheduling cleverness fixes the problem and buying becomes necessary. There's also a risk that the utilisation project drags on — scheduler work has a way of expanding — and we end up having spent three months and still needing hardware, having paid for the delay in user-visible latency incidents.
